[MATH: (4)/(5)|= (JK)/(60); JK|= 60 ⋅ (4)/(5); = 12 ⋅ 4; = 48.]

items.title: Finding the Perimeter of a Right Triangle Using Trigonometry

sections.normalized_html: In triangle [MATH: PQR,] angle [MATH: R] is a right angle and the length of [MATH: \overline{QR}] is [MATH: 24] units. If [MATH: \tan Q = \dfrac{5}{12},] what is the perimeter, in units, of triangle [MATH: PQR?]
sections.readable_text: In triangle [MATH: PQR,] angle [MATH: R] is a right angle and the length of [MATH: \overline{QR}] is [MATH: 24] units. If [MATH: \tan Q = \dfrac{5}{12},] what is the perimeter, in units, of triangle [MATH: PQR?]

sections.normalized_html:
First, since [MATH: \angle R] is a right angle, triangle [MATH: PQR] is a right triangle with the right angle at vertex [MATH: R,] which can be represented as follows:

We are told [MATH: \tan Q = \dfrac{5}{12}] and [MATH: QR = 24.] Using the definition of tangent, we have: [MATH: \tan Q|= (opposite)/(adjacent); (5)/(12)|= (PR)/(QR); (5)/(12)|= (PR)/(24); PR|= 24 ⋅ (5)/(12); = 10.]

To find the hypotenuse of the triangle, [MATH: \overline{PQ},] we apply the Pythagorean Theorem: [MATH: PQ|= sqrt((QR)^{2} + (PR)^{2}); = sqrt(24^{2} + 10^{2}); = sqrt(576 + 100); = sqrt(676); = 26]

Therefore, the perimeter of triangle [MATH: PQR] is [MATH: Perimeter|= PQ + PR + QR; = 26 + 10 + 24; = 60.]

If the area, in square units, of triangle [MATH: ABC] can be represented by the expression [MATH: k \tan 57^\circ,] where [MATH: k] is a constant, what is the value of [MATH: k?]

If the area, in square units, of triangle [MATH: ABC] can be represented by the expression [MATH: k \tan 57^\circ,] where [MATH: k] is a constant, what is the value of [MATH: k?]

sections.normalized_html:
We want to find the area of triangle [MATH: ABC] and express it in the form [MATH: k\tan 57^\circ.]

The area of a triangle is given by the formula: [MATH: \text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \text{base} \cdot \text{height}.]

Since triangle [MATH: ABC] is a right triangle with [MATH: \angle B = 90^\circ] and [MATH: \angle C = 57^\circ,] we can represent it as follows:

Now, we see that [MATH: \overline{AB}] is the base and [MATH: \overline{BC}] is the height, so the area of triangle [MATH: ABC] is [MATH: \text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot AB \cdot BC.]

Next, since [MATH: BC = 8] and [MATH: \angle C = 57^\circ,] we can find the length of [MATH: \overline{AB}] using the following trigonometric identity: [MATH: \tan ∠C|= (opposite)/(adjacent); \tan 57^{∘}|= (AB)/(BC); AB|= BC ⋅ \tan 57^{∘}; = 8\tan 57^{∘}]

Thus, the area is [MATH: Area|= (1)/(2) ⋅ AB ⋅ BC; = (1)/(2) ⋅ (8\tan 57^{∘}) ⋅ 8; = 32\tan 57^{∘}.]

Therefore, by comparing this with [MATH: k \tan 57^\circ,] we get [MATH: k = 32.]
